After the step, market-data-service cpu_pct is pinned at a near-constant high plateau (13:26 92.2, 13:30 92.21, 13:46 90.34, 14:00 85.23, 14:30 86.1; window max 94.51, mean 80.23) and does NOT track the gradually recovering hit ratio (10.82% -> 36.58% over the same interval). Market-data-service CPU therefore responds to the cache-miss state in both timing and sign, but the shape is a saturation clamp rather than a strictly proportional curve — consistent with CPU-bound quote rebuilds saturating cores (H1) while redis slowly refills.

market-data-service recorded ZERO restarts across every 60s bucket from 13:15Z to 13:25Z (min 0.0, max 0.0, mean 0.0, missing_points 0), so there is no process restart on market-data-service at the onset — its CPU step is not a restart/warm-up artifact.

redis-cache exposes no 'restarts' metric at all — query returned not_found with available_metrics = [connected_clients, cpu_pct, evictions_per_min, hit_ratio_pct, memory_pct] — so a redis-cache process/host restart event in 13:15-13:25Z cannot be measured from metrics; the only redis process-level evidence available is the log-level failover (tc-028), not a metric.

events.answer: Yes, other redis-cache consumers DO exist: the complete, non-truncated redis-cache upstream edge query (tc-049, partial:false) lists exactly four services with a cache edge to redis-cache — pricing-engine, market-data-service, auth-service and portfolio-service. Of the previously-truncated services, portfolio-service IS a confirmed redis-cache consumer (and also a downstream reader of market-data-service over http), while settlement-service and payment-service are definitively NOT redis-cache consumers (their only edges are kafka/ledger-db and bank-partner-api/ledger-db/kafka respectively) and order-service has no direct redis edge (it reaches redis only via pricing-engine). So H1's cold-cache storm is mechanically plausible across the four redis consumers, but the dependency graph exposes no key namespaces, so I cannot confirm whether auth-service and portfolio-service read the same quote:* keyspace as market-data-service/pricing-engine — that is the one open question.

events.title: redis-cache primary failure promoting an empty replica -> cold-cache miss storm -> market-data-service CPU-bound rebuilds -> pricing-engine deadline-exceeded
market-data-service self-inflicted CPU-saturation compute fault as the origin, with the redis failover a co-occurring symptom
External exchange-api / exchange-gateway degradation propagating into market-data-service
auth-service v7.2.0 deployment (11:30Z) indirectly affected pricing-engine

events.summary: Onset is solid and change history is cleanly excluded. H1's first hop (redis primary failed at 13:22:10Z, empty replica promoted, hit ratio 95.9%->10.8%) is now genuinely verified, not assumed, and the first market-data-service 'cache miss storm' WARN (13:22:25Z) post-dates the failover by 15s — a real sub-minute ordering favoring H1. But the ranking over H2 still cannot be settled with the data now available. H2 names a DIFFERENT origin (market-data-service self-saturation, hence a different fix) and is not contradicted by any measurement: market-data-service CPU steps with flat request_rate (~956 req/s), flat memory, zero restarts and zero ERROR logs, so no workload-proportional driver was ever measured. The single decisive discriminator the team itself posed — is the CPU burn proportional to redis miss volume, or pinned independent of redis state — is unresolved: F40 shows a saturation clamp that does not track the recovering hit ratio, which is consistent with either mechanism. The scope test is also blocked: redis reconnect storms imply many consumers, yet of the four confirmed cache-edge consumers (F43) auth-service is flat and portfolio-service — a redis consumer AND a downstream reader of the saturated market-data-service, the single most informative case — was never measured (budget exhausted). The one structural query that could bound the cold-cache storm (whether auth-service/portfolio-service read the same quote:* keyspace) is permanently unavailable (no namespace field, F48). With zero tool calls left and both the proportionality measurement and the portfolio-service/keyspace checks unobtainable, the evidence cannot separate H1 from H2. H1 is the better-supported single story (whichever way it resolves, redis failover is a genuine event and market-data-service's WARN names redis-cache), so I cap confidence at 0.55 rather than accept or drop it.
